pi.name: Paul F. Kramer
pi.title: Assistant Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Paul Kramer earned a B.A. in Psychology with a Neuroscience concentration from Grinnell College (2009) and a Ph.D. in Neuroscience from Oregon Health and Science University (2016), where he worked with John T. Williams. He completed postdoctoral training at the NIH with Zayd Khaliq studying dopaminergic axon physiology, including synaptic-like axo-axonal transmission from striatal cholinergic interneurons onto dopamine fibers. He opened his lab at the University of Michigan in August 2023 and received the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation Young Investigator Award in 2025 for nicotine research.

description: The Kramer Lab studies cellular and synaptic neurobiology in pursuit of new knowledge that will advance human health. Its overarching hypothesis is that axons have an active and unexplored role in neurotransmission: axons can compute information and generate output that contributes to behavior and to the etiology of neurological disease, much like the somatodendritic compartment. The lab focuses on dopaminergic axons in the striatum, how cholinergic and GABAergic inputs modulate them through axo-axonic transmission, and how this signaling is altered in substance use disorders (especially nicotine use disorder) and Parkinson's disease. In 2026 the lab received a NIDA-supported R01 to study the cellular mechanisms of nicotine use disorder.

areas.title: Axon physiology
areas.summary: The lab's central focus: how axons actively participate in neurotransmission and information processing, challenging the traditional view that limits neuronal computation to the cell body and dendrites.

areas.title: Axo-axonic transmission
areas.summary: Investigates communication between axons and neighboring axonal segments, including synaptic-like transmission from striatal cholinergic interneurons onto dopaminergic fibers.

areas.title: Substance use disorders
areas.summary: Examines how drugs of abuse, including nicotine, alter neuronal communication within brain reward circuitry.

areas.title: Parkinson's disease
areas.summary: Studies how disrupted dopaminergic neuronal signaling contributes to this neurodegenerative condition.

news.text: Recent U-M graduate and neuroscience major Sarah Wajdi joined the lab.
Jackie, Vin, and Lauren presented research at the Michigan Chapter of the Society for Neuroscience conference in Kalamazoo.
Qianyi Yu joins the lab, transitioning from the master's program to doctoral studies.
The lab received the notice of award for a NIDA-supported R01 to study the cellular mechanisms of nicotine use disorder.
Keira completed her Biology, Health and Society degree from the University of Michigan.
Lauren presented at the NIDA T32 year-end research update.
Dr. Lauren Madden joins the lab to study axonal computation, supported by a NIDA postdoctoral T32 fellowship.
Dr. Kramer received the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation Young Investigator Award for nicotine research.

joining: The lab welcomes graduate applicants from the Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology program (PhD or Master's) and the Neuroscience Graduate Program (PhD only). Candidates for postdoctoral and technical positions should reach out directly to Paul Kramer to inquire about available opportunities. Dr. Kramer emphasizes giving trainees foundational knowledge and tools to pursue shared research interests, and believes anyone driven by intrinsic motivation can become a scientist.
